Big lakes prove the rule from the other side: the Great Lakes, with fetches of hundreds of kilometers, produce genuinely dangerous storm waves that have sunk large ships.
Why can I see my breath on a cold day but not a warm one?

Your breath is always full of water vapor — the air leaving your lungs is warm (near body temperature) and essentially saturated with moisture. On a warm day that vapor stays invisible gas as it mixes with the surrounding air. On a cold day, the breath hits cold air that can hold far less water vapor, so the vapor immediately condenses into a cloud of microscopic liquid droplets — the same process that makes clouds and fog, in miniature. You are not seeing the vapor itself; you are seeing the tiny droplets it turned into. The colder and more humid the day, the denser and longer-lived the little cloud, which is why your breath is most dramatic on a frosty morning and gone entirely by summer.
Ice is clear, so why is snow white?

It is about how many surfaces the light meets. A single block of ice is mostly transparent because light passes through with few interruptions. Snow is ice shattered into millions of tiny crystals with air between them, and at every crystal surface some light is bounced and redirected. With that many bounces in every direction, all colors of light get scattered back to your eyes roughly equally — and equal amounts of all colors is what we perceive as white. It is the same reason crushed glass, foam, and powdered sugar look white despite being made of clear or colorless material. There is a lovely footnote: in very deep, compressed glacial ice, the air is squeezed out and the long path through pure ice lets the faint blue color of water itself show through, so glacier crevasses glow an intense blue — snow and glacier are the same substance at different densities.
Why does a hot air balloon rise? There's no engine pushing it up.

It floats, the way a beach ball floats in a pool — except the pool is the sky. Air expands when heated, so the air inside the balloon's envelope takes up more space per kilogram than the cooler air outside: it is less dense. The balloon displaces a large volume of that denser outside air, and the buoyant force equals the weight of the displaced air. When the inside air is hot enough that the whole craft — envelope, basket, people, and the hot air itself — weighs less than the cooler air it displaces, up it goes. The pilot steers vertically by adding heat to climb or letting the air cool to descend, and steers horizontally only by climbing or sinking to find wind blowing a different direction, since different altitudes often have different winds. No engine is needed because gravity and density do the work.
Why does a kettle whistle when the water boils?

The whistle is the sound of steam escaping through a deliberately bad exit. When water boils vigorously, it produces a large volume of steam that must leave the kettle. The spout's cap forces that steam through one or two small holes. As the fast jet of steam passes the hole's edge, it sheds little swirling eddies in a regular rhythm — the same vortex-shedding that makes a flag flap and wires hum in wind — and those rhythmic pressure pulses are sound waves. The pitch is set by the geometry of the whistle cap, which is why kettles sing at a fairly steady note rather than a roar. The whistle only starts at a rolling boil because gentle simmering does not produce steam fast enough to drive it. Engineers have actually used the kettle whistle as a model system for studying how jets of fluid generate tones.
Why does all food taste bland when I have a bad cold?

Because most of what you call taste is actually smell. Your tongue detects only the basics — sweet, salty, sour, bitter, umami, plus texture and temperature. The rich identity of food, the difference between strawberry and raspberry, comes from aroma molecules that travel from the back of your mouth up into your nasal cavity as you chew and swallow, a route called retronasal smell. A cold swells and mucus-coats exactly that passage, so the aroma molecules never reach the smell receptors. Your taste buds are working fine; the flavor channel is blocked. That is why pinching your nose makes a jelly bean taste like generic sweetness and why food 'comes back' suddenly the moment your congestion clears mid-meal. It is also why loss of smell, not loss of taste, is the symptom that devastates appetite when it persists.
How do cats manage to land on their feet when they fall?

With a maneuver called the righting reflex, run by the same inner-ear balance organs you have. A falling cat first senses which way is down. Then, because its spine is exceptionally flexible, it twists its body in two separate sections: the front half rotates to face downward first, then the rear half follows — by bending in the middle, the cat can rotate both halves without needing anything to push against, conserving angular momentum the way a figure skater manages a spin. The tail helps as a counterweight and fine adjuster, but tailless cats can still do it. The reflex appears in kittens at about six to seven weeks old. Two honest caveats: the cat needs a minimum drop — roughly 30 centimeters — to complete the rotation, and landing on feet is not the same as landing safely; falls from great heights still injure cats badly, even if their relatively low top speed in a fall (they spread out like a parachute) gives them better odds than most animals.
In class we did the ruler-drop reaction test. My five catches, in cm from the top of the ruler: 18, 22, 15, 25, 20. What was my reaction time?

First average your catches: (18 + 22 + 15 + 25 + 20) / 5 = 100 / 5 = 20 cm. A falling ruler accelerates under gravity, and the distance it falls relates to time by d = (1/2) g t², so t = sqrt(2d/g). With d = 0.20 m and g = 9.8 m/s²: t = sqrt(0.40 / 9.8) = sqrt(0.0408) ≈ 0.20 seconds. So your average reaction time is about 0.20 s, right in the typical human range of roughly 0.20-0.25 s for a visual reaction. Your individual trials ranged from 15 cm (≈ 0.17 s) to 25 cm (≈ 0.23 s), which is a normal spread — reaction time varies with attention moment to moment, which is exactly why the test averages several drops. Note the distance scale is not linear in time: the ruler falls slowly at first and faster later, so the gap between 0.20 s and 0.25 s on the ruler (about 11 cm) is much bigger than between 0.05 s and 0.10 s (about 4 cm). That is why small differences in catch distance at the high end mean less than they appear to.

I used a sound meter app around school and got these readings: library 35 dB, classroom during a lesson 55 dB, hallway between classes 60 dB, cafeteria 75 dB, gym during a pep rally 95 dB. How should I describe these in my report?

Start with the ranking, quietest to loudest: library 35, classroom 55, hallway 60, cafeteria 75, gym 95 dB. The key point for your report is that the decibel scale is logarithmic, not linear: every 10 dB increase represents roughly a doubling of perceived loudness (and ten times the sound intensity). So the cafeteria at 75 dB does not sound 'a bit louder' than the 55 dB classroom — it sounds about four times as loud. The gym at 95 dB sounds roughly sixteen times louder than the classroom and about sixty times louder than the library. Context anchors help readers: 35 dB is near a quiet bedroom, 55-60 dB is normal conversation level, and 75 dB is around a vacuum cleaner. The 95 dB pep rally deserves a health note: sustained exposure at 85 dB and above can damage hearing, though a short rally is far less risky than, say, a full concert at similar levels. One methods caveat: phone apps are uncalibrated, so your absolute numbers may be off by several dB — but since the same phone measured every location, the comparisons between places are still meaningful.
I measured the shadow of a 1-meter stick through the day: 9:00 -> 1.8 m, 11:00 -> 1.1 m, 13:00 -> 0.7 m, 15:00 -> 1.0 m, 17:00 -> 1.9 m. What pattern do you see?

A clean U-shape with the shortest shadow in the early afternoon. The shadow shrank all morning (1.8 → 1.1 → 0.7 m) as the Sun climbed higher in the sky, bottomed out at 0.7 m at 13:00, then lengthened again through the afternoon (1.0 → 1.9 m) as the Sun descended. Shadow length depends on the Sun's height: the higher the Sun, the shorter the shadow, so the minimum marks when the Sun was highest — your data put that at about 13:00, close to solar noon (which often falls a bit after clock noon because of time zones and daylight saving). The morning and afternoon are roughly symmetric: 11:00 (1.1 m) pairs with 15:00 (1.0 m), and 9:00 (1.8 m) with 17:00 (1.9 m), as expected if the Sun's path is symmetric around its peak. One thing your numbers cannot tell you alone is direction — if you had also noted which way the shadow pointed, you would see it sweep from west in the morning to east in the evening, the principle behind sundials.
Two identical shallow dishes each held 200 mL of water. One sat in full sun, one in shade, same day, same breeze. After two days: sun dish 120 mL, shade dish 165 mL. What happened and by how much?

Evaporation happened at two different rates. The sun dish lost 200 - 120 = 80 mL; the shade dish lost 200 - 165 = 35 mL. So the sunny dish evaporated a little more than twice as fast (80 vs 35 mL, a ratio of about 2.3). The mechanism: sunlight warmed the sun dish's water, and warmer water molecules move faster, so more of them have enough energy to escape the surface as vapor. Since the dishes were identical, side by side, and exposed to the same breeze, you controlled for wind and surface area — temperature is the variable left standing, which makes this a decent experiment design. The result matches everyday experience: puddles vanish faster on sunny days, and it is one reason farmers and gardeners care about shade and mulch for soil moisture. A useful follow-up would be to record the water temperature in each dish, which would let you tie the evaporation rate to temperature directly rather than to 'sun versus shade.'
Why does rubbing your hands together make them warm? Where does the heat come from?

From your muscles, converted by friction. When two surfaces slide against each other, friction resists the motion, and the kinetic energy of the sliding does not disappear — it is converted into thermal energy in the surfaces. Your hand muscles supply the motion energy (ultimately from food), your palms pay it out as heat at the contact surface, and the skin warms up. You can feel the conversion rate directly: rub slowly and gently and little happens; press harder and move faster and the warmth builds quickly, because you are doing more mechanical work per second against a larger friction force. It is the same physics, with the sign flipped, that makes brakes get hot stopping a car, makes a drill bit smoke in wood, and lets you start a fire with two sticks — friction is a machine for turning movement into heat, and your hands are just the friendliest version of it.
